specAnchors.text: understand why an increase in temperature results in an increase in the average speed of gas molecules
know that the Kelvin temperature of a gas is proportional to the average kinetic energy of its molecules

primer.text: A thermometer is a speedometer for molecules. Warm the gas and the average molecular speed rises; cool it and the swarm slows. Better still, the kelvin temperature is exactly proportional to the average kinetic energy — the proportionality that makes every gas law work.

modules.title: Temperature and molecular speed
modules.opening: Heat a sealed gas and the molecules do not drift in a preferred direction — they simply move faster in every direction. The speed distribution shifts upward: more molecules at every higher speed, same chaos, hotter gas.
keyPoints: Gas molecules move randomly with a range of speeds at any temperature.
Increasing the temperature increases the average speed of the molecules.
Heating transfers energy into the molecules' kinetic store.
The direction of molecular motion stays random as the speeds rise.
Cooling the gas lowers the average molecular speed.

low.restatement: Warm the gas, and its molecules zip about faster; chill it, and they slow. The directions stay random — only the pace changes with temperature.
low.analogy: A dance floor where the DJ raises the tempo: everyone keeps dancing every which way, but the whole crowd moves quicker.
low.examPointer: Say 'average speed increases' — individual molecules still vary, and the randomness of direction never becomes ordered flow.

medium.restatement: The molecules hold a spread of speeds described by a distribution, not a single value. Supplied energy raises the whole distribution: the mean speed grows, the spread widens, but the velocity vectors remain isotropic, so no bulk flow appears. The temperature rise is precisely the growth of mean translational kinetic energy.
medium.analogy: A crowded motorway at rush hour versus midnight: every car still picks its own lane and direction, but the average pace on the network rises with the 'temperature' of the traffic.
medium.examPointer: When explaining, connect the energy chain explicitly: heating → energy into molecular kinetic store → higher mean speed → (at fixed volume) harder, more frequent wall impacts.

modules.title: Kelvin temperature and average kinetic energy
modules.opening: The precise statement behind 'hotter means faster' is a proportionality: kelvin temperature and the mean kinetic energy of the molecules rise in lockstep. Double the kelvin temperature and the mean molecular energy doubles — the ladder every gas law climbs.
keyPoints: Kelvin temperature scales directly with the mean kinetic energy carried by the molecules.
At 0 K the average kinetic energy of the molecules is at its minimum.
Doubling the kelvin temperature doubles the average molecular kinetic energy.
The proportionality is why kelvin must be used in gas-law equations.
Average kinetic energy refers to the mean over all molecules, not to any single molecule.

low.restatement: Kelvin temperature and the molecules' average kinetic energy rise and fall together: double one and you double the other. At absolute zero that energy bottoms out.
low.analogy: A fuel gauge wired to the tank: the needle (temperature) and the fuel (energy) are locked together by design.
low.examPointer: Use the word 'proportional', not 'equal' — temperature is not the energy itself; it is proportional to it.

medium.restatement: The proportionality T ∝ mean translational KE is the kinetic definition of temperature, and it anchors why 0 K is unreachable-but-defined: it is the energy origin. Because the relation is linear through the true zero, temperature ratios in kelvin are energy ratios, which is exactly the property the pressure law and Charles-type arguments require.
medium.analogy: Staircases rising from the same ground floor: only from the common ground can 'twice as high' mean anything — and 0 K is that ground for molecular energy.
medium.examPointer: In evaporation questions, the survival chain is: the most energetic molecules leave, the average KE of the remainder falls, and since kelvin temperature is proportional to that average, the temperature falls. Quote all three links.

glossary.definition: The mean translational kinetic energy of a gas's molecules, proportional to kelvin temperature.
The average speed of the molecules, which rises with temperature and falls on cooling.
The spread of molecular speeds around the mean at any temperature.

workedExample.prompt: When a liquid evaporates, molecules escape from the surface of the liquid. What happens to the temperature of the liquid and the average kinetic energy of the molecules within it? A — both increase; B — both decrease; C — both stay the same; D — temperature decreases while average kinetic energy increases.
steps: Evaporation is selective: the most energetic molecules are the ones that leave the surface first.
With the energetic tail gone, the average kinetic energy per molecule of those remaining must decrease.
Options A and D fail because the average energy falls rather than rises or stays fixed.
Because kelvin temperature tracks the mean kinetic energy per molecule, the temperature falls too.
workedExample.finalAnswer: B — both the temperature of the liquid and the average kinetic energy of its remaining molecules decrease.
